title: Seed laboratory quality framework and seed testing legislation

lessons.title: The quality framework for seed laboratories
lessons.html:
Why a quality framework

A seed test result can decide whether a lot worth hundreds of thousands of rand is certified, exported or destroyed. Customers, regulators and trading partners must trust that the result is accurate, reproducible and traceable. A formal quality management system provides that trust by controlling every factor that can affect a result.

Standards and accreditation

  • ISTA Accreditation Standard: ISTA accredits seed laboratories that meet its standard and pass proficiency tests. Only accredited laboratories may issue ISTA International Seed Analysis Certificates.
  • ISO/IEC 17025: the general international standard for competence of testing and calibration laboratories. In South Africa, accreditation to this standard is granted by SANAS (South African National Accreditation System).

Core elements of the system

ElementWhat it controls
Document controlCurrent, approved versions of procedures and methods in use
Personnel competenceTraining, authorisation per test, ongoing monitoring
EquipmentCalibration, verification, maintenance, records
EnvironmentTemperature, humidity and light in germinators and work areas
MethodsValidated methods as per ISTA rules; deviations documented
Sample handlingReceipt, identification, storage, retention and disposal
Quality assuranceInternal checks, replicate agreement, proficiency tests
Records and reportingComplete, legible, traceable raw data and reports
Non-conformitiesDetection, root-cause analysis, corrective action
Internal audit and management reviewChecking the system works and improving it

Impartiality and confidentiality

Laboratory staff must not be influenced by commercial pressure from sales or production departments. Client information and results are confidential.

Measurement traceability

Balances, thermometers and moisture meters must be calibrated against references traceable to national or international standards, with certificates on file and intermediate checks between calibrations.

lessons.title: Seed testing legislation and compliance
lessons.html:
The legal setting

Seed testing does not happen in a vacuum. Results feed into legal obligations on seed sellers and into certification and export decisions.

National legislation

  • The Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and its regulations set requirements for the sale of seed, including minimum standards for germination and purity for prescribed kinds of plants, labelling requirements and the registration of persons and premises dealing in seed. A newer Plant Improvement Act was passed in 2018; confirm with your organisation which law and regulations currently apply.
  • The regulations specify that tests for compliance are done according to prescribed methods, generally aligned with the ISTA International Rules for Seed Testing.
  • Agricultural Pests Act 36 of 1983: phytosanitary requirements, relevant when seed is imported or exported and health tests are required.

International requirements

  • ISTA Rules: methods for sampling and testing, updated annually; laboratories must apply the current edition.
  • ISTA certificates: Orange certificates for lots sampled and tested by accredited bodies; Blue certificates for samples tested where the laboratory did not sample the lot.
  • OECD Seed Schemes: varietal certification for international trade, relying on laboratory results for lot quality.
  • Importing countries' phytosanitary requirements.

Labelling and declared values

Seed labels declare values such as germination and purity. Laboratories provide the results behind these declarations. Inspectors may sample seed in trade and test it; if results fall outside tolerance of the declared value or minimum standard, the seller may face legal action. This is why accuracy and traceability matter.

Laboratory compliance practice

  1. Keep a register of applicable legislation and rule editions, reviewed at least annually.
  2. Train staff on rule changes before they take effect.
  3. Retain samples and records for the periods required by law, ISTA and clients.
  4. Handle complaints and appeals through a documented process.
  5. Prepare for external audits by the accreditation body and inspections by authorities.

Key points

  • ISTA accreditation and ISO/IEC 17025 (via SANAS) underpin laboratory credibility.
  • A quality system controls documents, people, equipment, methods, samples and records.
  • National seed law sets minimum standards and labelling, using ISTA-aligned methods.
  • ISTA Orange and Blue certificates differ by who sampled the lot.
  • Keep legislation registers current and train staff on rule changes.
